-

CENTRE

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(
action for defamation
)

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

This is an action for defamation in which Mr. J.
is seeking compensatory damages of nearly $80,000 and punitive damages in the
amount of $10,000.

[
2
]

There are two defendants. One is the Jewish
Eldercare Centre (“JEC”), a long-term care centre where Mr. J.’s mother resided
from December 2013 until January 2015. The other is Ms. Mylène Auguste, who was
working as a beneficiary attendant at the JEC when the events out of which this
case arose took place.

*           *           *

[
3
]

On December 26, 2014, Ms. Auguste filed a report
in which she stated having just witnessed Mr. J. kissing his mother and
caressing her breasts while they were at the JEC’s cafeteria.
[1]
The report led to a police investigation which took place in January
2015.
[2]
No criminal charges were brought against Mr. J.

[
4
]

Four months later, in May 2015, a trial was held
in proceedings that had been commenced by the Quebec Public Curator (“QPC”) in
early 2014. The purpose of these proceedings was to institute a regime of
protective supervision, in the form of a curatorship, to both the person and
the property of Mr. J.’s mother.
[3]
Mr. J. contested the QPC’s application and asked the Court to
homologate a general power of attorney and a protection mandate through which
his mother had sought to appoint him as mandatary.
[4]

[
5
]

During the trial, which was presided by Justice
Gary D.D. Morrison, Ms. Auguste testified in relation to the events of
December 26, 2014.
[5]
Mr. J., who was represented by counsel at that time, also
testified.
[6]
He denied then, as he does now, Ms. Auguste’s allegations.

[
6
]

In his judgment granting the QPC’s application,
[7]
Justice Morrison found that the incident of December 26, 2014 had occurred
as described by Ms. Auguste.
[8]
He reached this conclusion after having found that she had been
“credible in her testimony regarding [Mr. J.] inappropriately kissing his
mother and touching her breasts through her clothing.”
[9]

[
7
]

Mr. J. filed an appeal of Justice Morrison’s
judgment.
[10]
However, his mother passed away in July 2015 and the appeal was
eventually abandoned.
[11]

*           *           *

[
8
]

The defendants contest Mr. J.’s action for
several reasons. First, they argue that it ought to be dismissed on grounds on
prescription. Second, they dispute Mr. J.’s assertion that Ms. Auguste
committed a fault when she reported the incident that allegedly occurred on
December 26, 2014 and later testified about it before Justice Morrison. The
defendants also contend that, in addition to being exaggerated, the damages claimed
by Mr. J. relate to injuries that were not caused by their alleged faults.

[
9
]

In my view, another question arises in this
matter, and it should logically be addressed at the outset. The question is
whether Mr. J. can relitigate the issue of whether the incident of
December 26, 2014 occurred as described by Ms. Auguste, given the conclusion
reached by Justice Morrison in May 2015.

*           *           *

[
10
]

Strictly speaking, Justice Morrison’s decision is
not binding in the present proceedings. The criteria of the doctrine of
res
judicata
, which are set out in article 2848
C.C.Q.
, are clearly
not met.

[
11
]

However, as the Court of Appeal recalled in 2018,
Quebec courts enjoy a discretionary power to prevent the relitigation of a previously
decided issue when doing so would amount to an abuse of procedure.
[12]
In its 2003 decision in
City of Toronto
, the Supreme Court
explained that this discretionary power engages “the inherent power of the
court to prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would . . . bring
the administration of justice into disrepute.”
[13]

[
12
]

In a day and age of scarce judicial resources,
where access to justice has become “the greatest challenge to the rule of law
in Canada”,
[14]

the longstanding objective of ensuring finality to litigation — which “requires
litigants to put their best foot forward to establish the truth of their
allegations when first called upon to do so”,
[15]
as
they should normally only “be entitled to one bite at the cherry”
[16]
—
has gained increased importance. Notably, the Court of Appeal’s 2018 decision suggests
that the burden rests on the party seeking to relitigate a previously decided
issue to show that an injustice would occur if he or she were not allowed to do
so.
[17]

[
13
]

In
City of Toronto
, the Supreme Court touched on the
circumstances under which it may be necessary to allow a party to relitigate a previously
decided issue:

The discretionary factors that apply to prevent the doctrine
of issue estoppel from operating in an unjust or unfair way are equally
available to prevent the doctrine of abuse of process from achieving a similar
undesirable result. There are many circumstances in which the bar against
relitigation, either through the doctrine of
res judicata
or that of
abuse of process, would create unfairness. If, for instance, the stakes in the
original proceeding were too minor to generate a full and robust response, while
the subsequent stakes were considerable, fairness would dictate that the
administration of justice would be better served by permitting the second
proceeding to go forward than by insisting that finality should prevail. An inadequate
incentive to defend, the discovery of new evidence in appropriate
circumstances, or a tainted original process may all overcome the interest in
maintaining the finality of the original decision […].

[
14
]

No such circumstances are present here. Mr. J. was represented by
counsel before and during the trial presided over by Justice Morrison. His
testimony in the present case to the effect that he was taken by surprise by
Ms. Auguste’s testimony on May 5, 2015 is not credible, as he must have been
well aware, prior to the May 2015 trial, that the QPC would rely on her account
of the events that occurred on December 26, 2014.
[18]
Furthermore, this is
not one of those cases where a party seeking to relitigate a previously decided
issue had little incentive to generate a full and robust response during the
first proceedings. Nor is this a case where the attempt to relitigate is based on
newly discovered evidence. Lastly, nothing suggests that the May 2015 trial was
unfair in any way.

[
15
]

In sum, all relevant factors point to denying Mr. J. the possibility of
relitigating the issue in the hope that the Court will reach a different
conclusion from the one reached by Justice Morrison regarding the events of December 26, 2014. His attempt to revisit this issue thus
constitutes an abuse of procedure.

[
16
]

Because the case turns on whether Ms. Auguste committed
a fault, and because she cannot possibly have done anything wrong by reporting sexual
misconduct directed at a JEC patient, Mr. J.’s action must
be dismissed.

*           *           *

[
17
]

By way of
obiter
, I note that the
defendants’ argument on the issue of fault is well founded.

[
18
]

In order to succeed in an action for defamation,
a plaintiff must first establish that “a reasonable person would [not] have
made the impugned remarks in the same context.”
[19]

While assessing this issue, courts must bear in mind that “[i]n every case,
determining fault is a contextual question of fact and circumstances.”
[20]

[
19
]

Mr. J.’s theory of the case is essentially that
Ms. Auguste’s false accusations regarding the December 26, 2014 incident were
made in retaliation for his frequent complaints about the appalling care his
mother received while she resided at the JEC. He considers those accusations to
fit within a broader pattern of unfounded or exaggerated allegations of
improper behaviour made against him by JEC staff members, and he adds that this
argument finds support in the fact that he never had any conflict with the
staff at CHSLD Vigi Mont-Royal, the long-term care centre where his mother was
transferred in mid-January 2015.
[21]
He
also points to the fact that no criminal charges were ever brought against him.

[
20
]

Undoubtedly, if Ms. Auguste did indeed fabricate
her account of the events that occurred on December 26, 2014, her conduct would
amount to a fault.

[
21
]

Mr. J. bears the burden of proof on this issue.
[22]
Furthermore, despite the nature of the allegations he makes against
Ms. Auguste, the standard of proof remains proof on a balance of probabilities.
[23]
This means that Mr. J. must demonstrate that it is more likely
than not that her account of the December 26, 2014 events is false and
fabricated.
[24]

[
22
]

After having heard both Ms. Auguste and Mr. J. —
and considered the remainder of the evidence that was adduced —, I am unable to
find her account of the events of December 26, 2014 to be false and fabricated.

[
23
]

There is no direct evidence supporting this
proposition. Mr. J.’s case is circumstantial, and his key allegation that his
mother received appalling care while at the JEC is supported only by his own
testimony. However, that testimony was not sufficiently probative to establish,
on a balance of probabilities, that the JEC somehow failed to properly care for
his mother. Significantly, the medical record dating from when his mother was
at the JEC, as well as Ms. Carole Mireault’s compelling testimony, show
that the frequent conflicts Mr. J. had with JEC staff members were much
more likely caused by his unwillingness to comply with applicable rules and
procedures than by legitimate concerns with the quality of the care received by
his mother.
[25]
Furthermore, Mr. J.’s assertion that he never had any conflict
with CHSLD Vigi Mont-Royal staff members — a fact which would tend to demonstrate
that the allegations of improper behaviour the JEC made against him before
December 26, 2014 were also false and fabricated —, is significantly
contradicted by his mother’s medical record.
[26]

[
24
]

In contrast, Ms. Auguste testified in a clear,
composed and compelling manner about the incident she witnessed on December 26,
2014. She is a disinterested witness whose account has generally remained
consistent since her initial report, which she completed less than an hour
after the incident took place.
[27]
Furthermore, the fact that Justice Morrison found her to be a credible
witness favours the defendants’ position.
[28]

[
25
]

As for the fact that no criminal charges were
brought against Mr. J. in relation to the events that occurred on December 26,
2014, it cannot — by and of itself — support a finding that Ms. Auguste fabricated
her account. Detective Sylvie Audette explained convincingly during her
testimony that a number of factors had led to the decision not to bring charges,
including the fact that Ms. Auguste — the sole witness of the alleged incident —
was unwilling to testify in criminal proceedings.
[29]

Another significant factor was the fact that Detective Audette was unable to
communicate with Mr. J.’s mother because of her severe cognitive
impairment.
[30]

[
26
]

In sum, Mr. J.’s case falls short of proving
that Ms. Auguste’s account of the events of December 26, 2014 was false
and fabricated. The more likely conclusion is that she acted in good faith
throughout this matter and that she consistently recalled the events she
witnessed on that day not only sincerely, but also accurately.

*           *           *

[
27
]

By way of further
obiter,
I am of the
view that the prescription defence raised by the defendants is not well founded.

[
28
]

Their argument is based on article 2929
C.C.Q.
,
which provides that “[a]n action for defamation is prescribed by one year from
the day on which the defamed person learned of the defamation/
[l]’action
fondée sur une atteinte à la réputation se prescrit par un an, à compter du
jour où la connaissance en fut acquise par la personne diffamée
.” As this
provision indicates, prescription begins to run when the plaintiff learns of
the allegedly defamatory comments, which is usually when he or she is in a
position to commence an action for defamation.
[31]

However, if the plaintiff is not initially aware of the identity of the impugned
comments’ authors, prescription will only begin to run on the day on which he
or she learns of that fact.
[32]

[
29
]

It is clear from Mr. J.’s originating
application, which was filed on May 4, 2016, that he is suing for injuries
resulting from the allegations made against him by Ms. Auguste in relation
to the events of December 26, 2014. His action must
thus be characterized as one for defamation.

[
30
]

The defendants are also right that Mr. J. could
have instituted an action for defamation well before May 4, 2015. He clearly
knew, as of January 2015, about the allegations made against him. He also knew that
they were having an impact on his reputation: that is clear from the
restrictions on his visiting rights that were imposed by CHSLD Vigi Mont-Royal
immediately upon his mother’s arrival.
[33]

Furthermore, Mr. J. admitted during his examination on discovery that the
allegations of sexual misconduct had damaged his reputation at CHSLD Vigi
Mont-Royal.
[34]
The evidence also clearly shows that Mr. J. was aware before
the May 2015 trial that Ms. Auguste was the JEC staff member who had filed
the report about the December 26, 2014 incident. He even admitted as much when
he testified in the current proceedings.
[35]

[
31
]

However, Mr. J. is not suing in relation to
injuries he allegedly suffered as a result of Ms. Auguste’s initial report,
made on December 26, 2014. As he indicated in his originating application and
further explained during the trial, he is rather suing in relation to injuries that
allegedly resulted from Ms. Auguste’s testimony before Justice Morrison. In
particular, a key aspect of his case is the allegation that Ms. Auguste’s
testimony was determinative in Justice Morrison’s decision to grant the QPC’s
application. Hence his position that prescription only started running on May
5, 2015, which is when Ms. Auguste testified.

[
32
]

The defendants respond that, when she testified
before Justice Morrison, Ms. Auguste merely reiterated her initial account
of the December 26, 2014 events. They add that the mere reiteration of
allegedly defamatory comments should not lead to the commencement of a new
prescription period. That may be so in some circumstances, but here Mr. J. is seeking damages in relation to distinct injuries he allegedly suffered
as a result of Ms. Auguste’s testimony in the May
2015 trial. Because Mr. J. could not possibly have sued in relation to
that allegedly injurious act before the curatorship trial took place, I would
not have dismissed his action on grounds of prescription.

*           *           *

[
33
]

Lastly — and again by way of
obiter
—, I
agree with the defendants that Mr. J. has not proved that Justice Morrison’s
decision would have been different had Ms. Auguste not testified as she did on
May 5, 2015. It is clear from the reasons issued by Justice Morrison
[36]
that his decision rested on many other factors, and there is no
basis to conclude that, in all likelihood, the QPC’s application would have
been dismissed had Ms. Auguste’s account of the events of December 26, 2014 not
been brought to his attention. Consequently, there is no causal link between the
defendants’ alleged faults and any injury suffered by Mr. J. as a result
of Justice Morrison’s decision.

WHEREFORE, THE COURT:

[
34
]

DISMISSES
the
plaintiff’s action;

[
35
]

WITH LEGAL COSTS
.

Mr. J.’s reputation, would she not have taken her plan to the next logical level
by agreeing to testify against him in criminal proceedings?
